narrative:
The model estimates a 25% chance that you will fail your final year, which is high enough that the school requires you to take remedial courses as a precaution.

The three factors that most strongly shaped this prediction were your number of past class failures, your desire to pursue higher education, and the size of your family. Surprisingly, having no previous failures was the strongest element pulling the prediction toward passing. Your clear ambition to continue studying beyond high school also pushed the outcome in a positive direction. However, coming from a smaller family (three or fewer members) worked against you; while most students who passed come from larger families (65.5% have more than three members), your situation is less common among those who succeed.

Taken together, these elements led the model to flag a noticeable risk of failure even though two of the top influences were working in your favor. The smaller family size appears to have outweighed the protective effects of your clean record and strong educational goals.

To improve your chances, focus on building consistent daily study habits—your current study time of less than two hours per week is lower than most successful students. Consider reaching out to your mother, who is your guardian, for more structured academic support at home, and look into free tutoring options now rather than waiting. Small, steady improvements in study routine can meaningfully shift your trajectory before the final exams. (248 words)
